questions.prompt: What is the core problem in halo effect?
choices: One visible trait spreads into unrelated judgments
Every first impression is false
No trait ever provides any information

explanation.gentle: Yes. The first cue is spreading too far.
explanation.direct: Correct. A salient trait is organizing broader evaluation beyond what it proves.
explanation.competitive: That is the scam. One cue is counterfeiting the rest of the file.

choices: Because one strong impression feels easier than separate careful judgments
Because one trait always proves every other trait
Because first impressions are all the evidence you need

explanation.gentle: Right. One strong cue is easy for the mind to carry.
explanation.direct: Exactly. Coherent broad impressions feel simpler than independent evaluation.
explanation.competitive: That is it. The brain likes one clean story more than real paperwork.

questions.prompt: Which example best fits halo effect?
choices: A polished candidate is assumed to be more competent in unrelated ways
A candidate answers one technical question correctly
A manager reads a project report twice

explanation.gentle: Yes. One trait is spilling into broader judgment.
explanation.direct: Correct. Presentation quality is being allowed to stand in for unrelated competence evidence.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. The polish is smuggling fake credentials across the border.

questions.prompt: A beautiful product feels higher quality before testing. What is the better move?
choices: Separate visual appeal from evidence about actual quality
Assume beauty is enough proof of performance
Ignore all impressions completely

explanation.gentle: Yes. The attractive feature should be kept separate from quality claims.
explanation.direct: Correct. Aesthetic appeal may be real, but it is not sufficient proof of build quality.
explanation.competitive: That is the move. Take the glamour off the spec sheet and see what survives.

questions.prompt: What boundary matters in this chapter?
choices: The first trait may be real even though the broader spillover is not justified
All first impressions should be ignored
Positive traits never spill over, only negative ones do

explanation.gentle: Right. The problem is not the first cue itself, but how far it spreads.
explanation.direct: Exactly. The chapter questions spillover, not the existence of the original signal.
explanation.competitive: Yes. The cue can be real without getting to annex the whole map.

questions.prompt: Why can one visible flaw distort judgment so strongly?
choices: Because dislike can spill into unrelated evaluation just like admiration can
Because one flaw proves every negative conclusion
Because flaws matter more than evidence

explanation.gentle: Yes. Negative spillover is part of the same bias.
explanation.direct: Correct. One flaw can unfairly contaminate broader judgments beyond its actual scope.
explanation.competitive: That is the bruise. The stain can counterfeit evidence just as well as the glow can.

questions.prompt: What is the hard diagnostic question in this chapter?
choices: What am I inferring here that the original visible trait does not actually prove?
How can I strengthen my first impression faster?
Why should I reject every initial signal immediately?

explanation.gentle: Yes. The goal is to separate observation from unsupported inference.
explanation.direct: Correct. Each added conclusion should have its own evidence.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Make the stowaway claims show their paperwork.

questions.prompt: Why does halo effect distort decisions and not just impressions?
choices: Because one trait can influence hiring, grading, trust, and purchasing beyond the evidence
Because impressions never affect behavior
Because decisions are always purely rational

explanation.gentle: Right. Broader decisions can start resting on spillover.
explanation.direct: Exactly. Once one cue takes over evaluation, real outcomes get driven by borrowed authority.
explanation.competitive: That is the damage. One flashy cue starts steering real money, trust, and status.

questions.prompt: Which response best counters halo effect?
choices: Split the original observation from each extra inference and demand separate evidence
Trust the strongest first impression
Assume every broad impression is accurate if it feels coherent

explanation.gentle: Yes. Each extra claim needs its own support.
explanation.direct: Correct. Better judgment prevents one cue from doing illegitimate extra work.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Break the fused verdict apart and make every claim carry its own receipts.

questions.prompt: What distinction does this chapter ask you to preserve?
choices: A visible trait is different from the broader verdict you are tempted to build from it
One signal and the whole file are the same thing
If a trait stands out, it should govern all judgments

explanation.gentle: Right. One cue is not the entire person or object.
explanation.direct: Correct. The chapter protects the difference between direct evidence and halo spillover.
explanation.competitive: That is the split. One signal is not a legal takeover of the whole file.
